amendments.rule: A verbless clause supplies its English copula from the construction, not from nothing. In *that it was good*, the supplied *it was* belongs to the unit headed on `טוֹב`; do not mark it `added`. **Where the ASV renders a verbless clause with a presentative *there was* or *there were*, the dummy *there* is part of the same construction-supplied frame as the copula and joins the unit that bears that copula under this rule.** It is never `added`, and the unit still heads on its lexical predicate or anchor. **The anchor may be of any kind, since what licenses the dummy is the presentative frame the construction supplies and not the part of speech the frame is built on.** A nominal anchor, a prepositional predicate and an adverbial anchor are read alike: `וְעוֹד חָמֵשְׁ שָׁנִים` → *and* ***there are yet*** *five years* gives *there are yet* to `עוֹד`, headed on *yet*, and the numeral phrase keeps its own English. Do not read the list as closed and mark the dummy `added` because the anchor is neither a noun nor a preposition; the sentence above says it is never `added`, and rule 17 puts the same dummy on a finite verb and rule 50 on an existential `אַיִן`. **But the dummy this sentence governs is the presentative *there* and no other.** A cleft or impersonal *it* the ASV writes in such a clause — *it was not you that sent me hither*, *It is enough* — is not a presentative frame and no morpheme licenses it, so it is its own `added` unit under rule 30, exactly as the supplied lexical verb of the next sentence is. **And where the ASV clefts a clause, the whole English frame goes the same way.** A cleft writes a dummy *it*, a copula, and a relative before the clause that carries the predication, and where the Hebrew writes a finite verb for that predication no morpheme answers to any of the three: the dummy and its copula are one `added` unit headed on the copula, and the cleft relative is its own `added` unit under rule 55, which marks a subordinator the ASV has written over a clause no written subordinator reaches. The copula is not this rule's construction-supplied one, because the test below asks which morpheme is there to carry the English and a clause whose predication a written verb already carries licenses no copula; and the relative is not rule 46's, because that rule supplies a relative to make a participle or a headless clause into a noun phrase, whereas a clefted nominal the ASV has already rendered is a written antecedent with a finite clause juxtaposed to it, which rule 46 excludes in its own terms. `לֹא־רַבִּים יֶחְכָּמוּ` → ***It is*** *not the great* ***that*** *are wise* gives *not* to the negative, *the great* to the substantival adjective under rule 46 and *are wise* to the finite verb, leaving *It is* and *that* `added`. Read what stands in the Hebrew before marking any of the three: a written `אֲשֶׁר` takes the relative under rule 46's first rider, an explicit pronoun takes a *that* the ASV writes for it under rule 18, and where the clefted clause is itself verbless the copula is the predicate's under the sentences below and only the dummy and the relative are supplied. **Apart from that presentative dummy, this covers the copula and nothing more.** Where the ASV instead supplies a whole *lexical* verb for a clause whose Hebrew has none — the allotment formula `וְלִבְנֵי קְהָת הַנּוֹתָרִים ... עָרִים עָשֶׂר` → *And unto the rest of the sons of Kohath* ***were given*** *by lot ... ten cities* — no morpheme's rendering that verb completes, and it is `added` under rule 30, together with any object the ASV supplies alongside it, as in *were given them*. Test by asking which morpheme is there to carry the English: `הָיָה` carries the *have* of rule 43 and the frame of rule 21, a Hebrew verb carries the light verb of rule 44, and a preposition that is itself the predicate carries the copula of rule 49 — but a preposition the ASV has already spent a word on, as in *unto the rest*, carries nothing further, and a clause with no verb in it at all licenses no verb. **But the copula is whatever verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand, and not the word *be* alone.** English links a subject to its predicate with *seem*, *become*, *prove*, *remain* and *come* as readily as with *be*, and such a verb is the construction-supplied copula of this rule rather than a supplied lexical verb: it joins the unit of the predicate morpheme it links, which keeps its own English beside it, and that unit still heads on the word carrying the predicate's lexeme under rule 24 rather than on the linking verb. `וּגְדוֹלָה הִיא אֵלָי` → *and it* ***seemed*** *great unto me* gives *seemed great* to `גָּדוֹל`, headed on *great*, while `הִיא` keeps only its own *it*; `הַכֹּל כַּאֲשֶׁר לַכֹּל` → *All things* ***come*** *alike to all* gives *come alike* to the `כַּאֲשֶׁר` that is the clause's predicate, headed on *alike*. This is rule 49's reading of `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which* ***belonged to*** *the house* and of a resultative `לְ` → *shalt become*, holding for a predicate of any kind and not only a prepositional one, and rule 30 already states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of a fused expression does not defeat its one-rendering condition. What tells such a verb from the supplied lexical verb of the preceding sentences is whether a predicate morpheme stands in the clause for it to link: a linking verb stands beside that predicate's own English and adds no participant the Hebrew does not write, whereas *were given* introduces an event and an agent the Hebrew never wrote, and rule 34's *cheweth* stands in a line whose predicate the Hebrew leaves unwritten altogether. Test by subtraction as rules 16, 31 and 43 do — drop the English verb and ask whether what has gone is the link English writes for a predication the Hebrew already made, or the predication itself. **The same lexical-verb boundary holds inside a nominal recasting.** A construct relation can license the English preposition used for it, but not a supplied lexical participle: `חֲמַס אֶרֶץ` → *violence done to the land* gives *violence* to the construct noun and *to the land* to its dependent under rule 19, while *done* is `added` because no source verb licenses it. This is not rule 31's generic completion of a substantive's lexeme: *done* predicates an event of the violence rather than naming the violence. **The copula goes to the predicate, and where a predicate morpheme is present an explicit subject takes only its own English.** Where the clause writes its subject — a pronoun such as `אָנֹכִי`, `אֲנִי`, `אַתְּ` or `הוּא`, or a subject noun — that morpheme takes the English pronoun or noun realizing it and nothing more, while the supplied *am*, *art*, *is*, *are* or *was* joins the predicate, exactly as rule 49 puts it on the preposition heading a prepositional predicate and rule 34 puts it on the predicate a gapped line licenses. `עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם אָנֹכִי` → *I* ***am*** *Abraham's servant* gives *am* to `עֶבֶד` and *I* to `אָנֹכִי`; `בַת מִי אַתְּ` → *Whose daughter* ***art*** *thou* gives *art* to `בַת`; `הוּא אֲדֹנִי` → *It* ***is*** *my master* gives *is* to `אֲדֹנִי`; and `מִי הָאִישׁ הַלָּזֶה` → *What man* ***is*** *this* gives *is* to `מִי`, which is the clause's predicate, leaving *this* to the demonstrative. **A tripartite clause whose resuming pronoun the ASV renders by nothing but that copula is read on those same terms.** Where the clause writes a subject noun and resumes it with `הוּא`, `הִיא` or `הֵמָּה` before the predicate, and the ASV realizes the subject once by the noun, the resuming pronoun is the unrendered occurrence and is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 22, while the copula joins the predicate as the preceding sentences direct, discontinuous around a possessive or an article under rule 25: `יְהוָה הוּא נַחֲלָתוֹ` → *Jehovah* ***is*** *their* ***inheritance*** gives *is inheritance* to `נַחֲלָה` and leaves `הוּא` nothing. Do not give the copula to that pronoun on the ground that a present morpheme takes its English before a construction-supplied reading: what that reasoning governs, in rules 46, 47 and 48, is an English word some morpheme's own sense answers to, and a copula answers to the predication rather than to the pronoun, which is why this rule sends it to the predicate wherever a predicate morpheme stands. Where instead the ASV writes a word of its own for the pronoun — `הוּא הַדָּבָר` → ***that*** *is the thing* — that pronoun is holding an English word already and is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and the copula still joins the predicate. One chapter may write both shapes, and DEU.18.2 and DEU.18.22 do. **But the predicate morpheme that sentence looks for is one free to bear the copula, and a predicate that is itself a clause is not.** Where the predicate of such a tripartite clause is a relative or headless relative clause whose written finite verb already carries its own predication, no morpheme in it is available to take the matrix copula: assigning the word to that verb would leave one Hebrew verb holding two English clauses, which rule 17 refuses for the same reason in its matrix duration frame, and the resuming pronoun is then the clause's only overt anchor and takes the copula, exactly as an explicit subject does where the predicate is wholly elided. `מַה־שֶּׁהָיָה הוּא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה` → *That which hath been* ***is*** *that which shall be* gives *is* to `הוּא`, while `שֶׁ` keeps the *that which* rule 46's first rider gives it and `יִּהְיֶה` keeps its own *shall be*. Read what the predicate is before applying the preceding paragraph: a nominal, adjectival or prepositional predicate is free to take the copula and the pronoun is `unrepresented` as before, and one chapter may write both shapes, as ECC.1.9 and ECC.1.17 do. **Where the predicate is wholly elided and no predicate morpheme is available to bear the construction-supplied copula, the copula instead joins the explicit subject as the clause's sole overt anchor:** `אֲנִי` → *I am*. This exception does not apply where a predicate is written. **And a copula the ASV fronts as a question auxiliary belongs to the interrogative particle, not to the predicate.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question, stands in a verbless clause and the ASV writes a single *Is*, *Am*, *Art*, *Are* or *Was* at the clause head, that one word is both this rule's construction-supplied copula and the question auxiliary rule 17 gives the particle: the particle takes it and heads on it, and the predicate keeps only its own English. `הֲלֹא יִרְאָתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ` → ***Is*** *not thy fear of God thy confidence* gives *Is* to `הֲ` and leaves `כִּסְלָה` the bare *confidence*. This is rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause holding for a verbless clause with any predicate, and rule 17's *belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb* holding where there is no verb to compete for the word. Where the ASV writes a second copula for the predicate itself, that one is the predicate's under this rule's earlier sentences; where no interrogative morpheme stands in the clause, there is no particle to take it and those sentences govern alone. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, since the copula stands beside the subject in every one of these; where the predicate's own words then stand apart from it, the unit is discontinuous under rule 25. **Rule 20 also governs an identifying formula where the ASV repeats one subject pronoun as both an English subject demonstrative and a predicate determiner.** Both realizations belong to that pronoun in one discontinuous unit, while the copula still goes to the written predicate: `הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה` → *These are that Aaron and Moses* gives *These ... that* to `הוּא`, headed on *These*, and *are Aaron* to `אַהֲרֹן`. The repeated demonstrative is not `added`; it is the ASV's emphatic identifying expansion of the single pronoun.
amendments.why: Rule 20's tripartite paragraph assumes the predicate morpheme is free to take the copula, and its 'Do not give the copula to that pronoun' is stated without qualification. ECC.1.9 is the case it had not considered: `מַה־שֶּׁהָיָה הוּא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה` and `מַה־שֶּׁנַּעֲשָׂה הוּא שֶׁיֵּעָשֶׂה`, where the predicate is a headless relative clause whose finite verb already holds *shall be* and *shall be done*. Read literally, the rule sends the matrix *is* into that subordinate verb's unit, giving one Hebrew verb two English clauses — the outcome rule 17's matrix duration frame paragraph refuses in as many words, and the reason rule 20 itself already carves out the wholly-elided predicate. The amendment adds that carve-out and nothing else: the ordinary nominal and adjectival cases, which are what the corpus records and what ECC.1.10 and ECC.1.17 are, are untouched, and the new sentences cannot fire where no clausal predicate stands. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule so the unqualified prohibition is corrected where a reader meets it. Evidence: ECC.1.9's two units, plus the structural argument from rules 17 and 20's own elided-predicate exception; the corpus tables supplied contradict neither, showing no treatment of a resumptive הוּא in a clause with a clausal predicate.

conventions: Positive existential יֵשׁ is read as rule 50 reads the Aramaic אִיתַי: it takes whatever overt finite frame the ASV writes for it, a dummy *there* joins that unit as it does an אַיִן's, and the unit heads on the finite word rather than on the dummy. ECC.1.10 יֵשׁ דָּבָר → *Is there a thing* gives *Is there* to יֵשׁ, headed on *Is*. Rule 50 names אַיִן, אֶפֶס and אִיתַי but not the Hebrew positive particle, so this is recorded rather than inferred; the question is marked by inversion alone and no הֲ stands in the clause to claim the fronted word under rule 17.

Read what stands in the Hebrew before marking any of the three: a written `אֲשֶׁר` takes the relative under rule 46's first rider, an explicit pronoun takes a *that* the ASV writes for it under rule 18, and where the clefted clause is itself verbless the copula is the predicate's under the sentences below and only the dummy and the relative are supplied. **Apart from that presentative dummy, this covers the copula and nothing more.** Where the ASV instead supplies a whole *lexical* verb for a clause whose Hebrew has none — the allotment formula `וְלִבְנֵי קְהָת הַנּוֹתָרִים ... עָרִים עָשֶׂר` → *And unto the rest of the sons of Kohath* ***were given*** *by lot ... ten cities* — no morpheme's rendering that verb completes, and it is `added` under rule 30, together with any object the ASV supplies alongside it, as in *were given them*. Test by asking which morpheme is there to carry the English: `הָיָה` carries the *have* of rule 43 and the frame of rule 21, a Hebrew verb carries the light verb of rule 44, and a preposition that is itself the predicate carries the copula of rule 49 — but a preposition the ASV has already spent a word on, as in *unto the rest*, carries nothing further, and a clause with no verb in it at all licenses no verb. **But the copula is whatever verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand, and not the word *be* alone.** English links a subject to its predicate with *seem*, *become*, *prove*, *remain* and *come* as readily as with *be*, and such a verb is the construction-supplied copula of this rule rather than a supplied lexical verb: it joins the unit of the predicate morpheme it links, which keeps its own English beside it, and that unit still heads on the word carrying the predicate's lexeme under rule 24 rather than on the linking verb. `וּגְדוֹלָה הִיא אֵלָי` → *and it* ***seemed*** *great unto me* gives *seemed great* to `גָּדוֹל`, headed on *great*, while `הִיא` keeps only its own *it*; `הַכֹּל כַּאֲשֶׁר לַכֹּל` → *All things* ***come*** *alike to all* gives *come alike* to the `כַּאֲשֶׁר` that is the clause's predicate, headed on *alike*. This is rule 49's reading of `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which* ***belonged to*** *the house* and of a resultative `לְ` → *shalt become*, holding for a predicate of any kind and not only a prepositional one, and rule 30 already states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of a fused expression does not defeat its one-rendering condition. What tells such a verb from the supplied lexical verb of the preceding sentences is whether a predicate morpheme stands in the clause for it to link: a linking verb stands beside that predicate's own English and adds no participant the Hebrew does not write, whereas *were given* introduces an event and an agent the Hebrew never wrote, and rule 34's *cheweth* stands in a line whose predicate the Hebrew leaves unwritten altogether. Test by subtraction as rules 16, 31 and 43 do — drop the English verb and ask whether what has gone is the link English writes for a predication the Hebrew already made, or the predication itself. **The same lexical-verb boundary holds inside a nominal recasting.** A construct relation can license the English preposition used for it, but not a supplied lexical participle: `חֲמַס אֶרֶץ` → *violence done to the land* gives *violence* to the construct noun and *to the land* to its dependent under rule 19, while *done* is `added` because no source verb licenses it. This is not rule 31's generic completion of a substantive's lexeme: *done* predicates an event of the violence rather than naming the violence. **The copula goes to the predicate, and where a predicate morpheme is present an explicit subject takes only its own English.** Where the clause writes its subject — a pronoun such as `אָנֹכִי`, `אֲנִי`, `אַתְּ` or `הוּא`, or a subject noun — that morpheme takes the English pronoun or noun realizing it and nothing more, while the supplied *am*, *art*, *is*, *are* or *was* joins the predicate, exactly as rule 49 puts it on the preposition heading a prepositional predicate and rule 34 puts it on the predicate a gapped line licenses. `עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם אָנֹכִי` → *I* ***am*** *Abraham's servant* gives *am* to `עֶבֶד` and *I* to `אָנֹכִי`; `בַת מִי אַתְּ` → *Whose daughter* ***art*** *thou* gives *art* to `בַת`; `הוּא אֲדֹנִי` → *It* ***is*** *my master* gives *is* to `אֲדֹנִי`; and `מִי הָאִישׁ הַלָּזֶה` → *What man* ***is*** *this* gives *is* to `מִי`, which is the clause's predicate, leaving *this* to the demonstrative. **A tripartite clause whose resuming pronoun the ASV renders by nothing but that copula is read on those same terms.** Where the clause writes a subject noun and resumes it with `הוּא`, `הִיא` or `הֵמָּה` before the predicate, and the ASV realizes the subject once by the noun, the resuming pronoun is the unrendered occurrence and is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 22, while the copula joins the predicate as the preceding sentences direct, discontinuous around a possessive or an article under rule 25: `יְהוָה הוּא נַחֲלָתוֹ` → *Jehovah* ***is*** *their* ***inheritance*** gives *is inheritance* to `נַחֲלָה` and leaves `הוּא` nothing. Do not give the copula to that pronoun on the ground that a present morpheme takes its English before a construction-supplied reading: what that reasoning governs, in rules 46, 47 and 48, is an English word some morpheme's own sense answers to, and a copula answers to the predication rather than to the pronoun, which is why this rule sends it to the predicate wherever a predicate morpheme stands. Where instead the ASV writes a word of its own for the pronoun — `הוּא הַדָּבָר` → ***that*** *is the thing* — that pronoun is holding an English word already and is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and the copula still joins the predicate. One chapter may write both shapes, and DEU.18.2 and DEU.18.22 do. **But the predicate morpheme that sentence looks for is one free to bear the copula, and a predicate that is itself a clause is not.** Where the predicate of such a tripartite clause is a relative or headless relative clause whose written finite verb already carries its own predication, no morpheme in it is available to take the matrix copula: assigning the word to that verb would leave one Hebrew verb holding two English clauses, which rule 17 refuses for the same reason in its matrix duration frame, and the resuming pronoun is then the clause's only overt anchor and takes the copula, exactly as an explicit subject does where the predicate is wholly elided. `מַה־שֶּׁהָיָה הוּא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה` → *That which hath been* ***is*** *that which shall be* gives *is* to `הוּא`, while `שֶׁ` keeps the *that which* rule 46's first rider gives it and `יִּהְיֶה` keeps its own *shall be*. Read what the predicate is before applying the preceding paragraph: a nominal, adjectival or prepositional predicate is free to take the copula and the pronoun is `unrepresented` as before, and one chapter may write both shapes, as ECC.1.9 and ECC.1.17 do. **Where the predicate is wholly elided and no predicate morpheme is available to bear the construction-supplied copula, the copula instead joins the explicit subject as the clause's sole overt anchor:** `אֲנִי` → *I am*. This exception does not apply where a predicate is written. **And a copula the ASV fronts as a question auxiliary belongs to the interrogative particle, not to the predicate.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question, stands in a verbless clause and the ASV writes a single *Is*, *Am*, *Art*, *Are* or *Was* at the clause head, that one word is both this rule's construction-supplied copula and the question auxiliary rule 17 gives the particle: the particle takes it and heads on it, and the predicate keeps only its own English. `הֲלֹא יִרְאָתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ` → ***Is*** *not thy fear of God thy confidence* gives *Is* to `הֲ` and leaves `כִּסְלָה` the bare *confidence*. This is rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause holding for a verbless clause with any predicate, and rule 17's *belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb* holding where there is no verb to compete for the word. Where the ASV writes a second copula for the predicate itself, that one is the predicate's under this rule's earlier sentences; where no interrogative morpheme stands in the clause, there is no particle to take it and those sentences govern alone. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, since the copula stands beside the subject in every one of these; where the predicate's own words then stand apart from it, the unit is discontinuous under rule 25. **Rule 20 also governs an identifying formula where the ASV repeats one subject pronoun as both an English subject demonstrative and a predicate determiner.** Both realizations belong to that pronoun in one discontinuous unit, while the copula still goes to the written predicate: `הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה` → *These are that Aaron and Moses* gives *These ... that* to `הוּא`, headed on *These*, and *are Aaron* to `אַהֲרֹן`. The repeated demonstrative is not `added`; it is the ASV's emphatic identifying expansion of the single pronoun.
amended.why: Rule 20's tripartite paragraph assumes the predicate morpheme is free to take the copula, and its 'Do not give the copula to that pronoun' is stated without qualification. ECC.1.9 is the case it had not considered: `מַה־שֶּׁהָיָה הוּא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה` and `מַה־שֶּׁנַּעֲשָׂה הוּא שֶׁיֵּעָשֶׂה`, where the predicate is a headless relative clause whose finite verb already holds *shall be* and *shall be done*. Read literally, the rule sends the matrix *is* into that subordinate verb's unit, giving one Hebrew verb two English clauses — the outcome rule 17's matrix duration frame paragraph refuses in as many words, and the reason rule 20 itself already carves out the wholly-elided predicate. The amendment adds that carve-out and nothing else: the ordinary nominal and adjectival cases, which are what the corpus records and what ECC.1.10 and ECC.1.17 are, are untouched, and the new sentences cannot fire where no clausal predicate stands. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule so the unqualified prohibition is corrected where a reader meets it. Evidence: ECC.1.9's two units, plus the structural argument from rules 17 and 20's own elided-predicate exception; the corpus tables supplied contradict neither, showing no treatment of a resumptive הוּא in a clause with a clausal predicate.

report: Checked all 41 candidate lemma groups. Every multi-treatment bucket is licensed either by what the ASV actually writes (a *the* written or not for הַ; and/but/yet/also/yea for וְ; to/unto/into/toward for אֶל; concerning/above/over/in/to for עַל) or by a difference the Hebrew writes (a לְ present or absent before the infinitive — 1.13 and 1.17 s006 against 1.17 s010, which is rule 52's closing sentence; a כֹּל present in 1.9 and absent in 1.11, which is why *no* fuses there under rule 35 while *any* joins the noun here under rule 15). None of these is a split.

The one construction analysed two ways is the tripartite subject–הוּא–predicate clause, and the difference is in the source. ECC.1.10 (זֶה חָדָשׁ הוּא) and ECC.1.17 (זֶה הוּא רַעְיוֹן רוּחַ) leave הוּא unrepresented and put the copula on an adjectival or nominal predicate, which is rule 20's tripartite sentence exactly. ECC.1.9 gives *is* to each הוּא because there the predicate is itself a headless relative clause whose written finite verb already holds *shall be* and *shall be done*; sending the matrix copula into that verb would leave one Hebrew verb holding two English clauses, which rule 17 refuses in its matrix-frame paragraph. Both verses named the competing reading. The edges are kept and rule 20 is amended instead, so its flat prohibition on giving the copula to the resuming pronoun is not read as reaching a clausal predicate.

Added-unit sweep, since the candidate table is blind to `added`: the chapter has five — *its* and *again* (1.6), the italic *it* (1.8), the relative *that* (1.13), *me* (1.16). Supplied object pronouns are `added` in both places they occur (1.8, 1.16, rule 44); supplied determiners and construction-supplied copulas are `added` nowhere in the chapter; and a supplied relative is `added` only where the Hebrew writes the antecedent and juxtaposes a finite clause (1.13, rules 46 and 55), while it joins the unit in 1.9, 1.11, 1.15 and 1.18, where the clause or the nominal is what the English noun phrase is built on. That boundary is held consistently.

*goeth down* (1.5) keeps its particle while *again* (1.6) is `added`: the same rule 44 subtraction, different lexemes — *goeth* alone does not write בּוֹא's setting, whereas *returneth* has already written שׁוּב's returning. ECC.1.7 renders שָׁבִים by *again* itself, the infinitive keeping *go*, so all three treatments of שׁוּב answer to what the ASV wrote and none is a split.

BSB: all sixteen disagreements are documented convention differences and none is a genuine error. Four articles for which the ASV writes no *the* (1.2, 1.8, 1.13, 1.14; rule 29); five לְ before infinitives for which it writes no function word, three of them after *cannot*, whose complement English writes bare (1.7, 1.8, 1.11, 1.15; rules 40 and 52); the suffix of אֵינֶנּוּ, whose subject the ASV writes as *the sea* (1.7; rules 22, 50); the resuming הוּא of 1.10 and 1.17 (rule 20); גַּם in 1.11, which the *neither* there does not carry, that word being the corpus-standard וְ + לֹא fusion recorded in 400+ units; לָהֶם in 1.11, silenced by the recasting (rule 40); the waw of 1.16, left unrendered in the ASV's compressed *have gotten ... great*; and the cohortative he of 1.17 (rule 32).

MACULA's gloss on ECC.1.17 אֶתְּנָה distributes the word's gloss in reverse — *I* on the verb, *gave* on the Sh — which is exactly rule 39's display defect and is what BSB's 'represented' status for that token reflects. The morphology is what the verse read, and the he is unrepresented under rule 32. Flagged so a later reader does not treat the gloss as evidence.

Large-source-unit candidate checked and kept: ECC.1.10 unit 15, מִלִּפְנֵי → *before*, three morphemes. Rule 30 fuses the two prepositions with the construct noun on its one-rendering condition, headed on the construct under rule 23, with the suffix aligned separately to *us* under rule 18. Nothing in the English writes פָּנֶה's own lexeme, so rule 2 does not split it.
